claim: HVC is necessary for singing in zebra finches.
source: One site where feedback could interact with song motor commands is the sensorimotor nucleus HVC, which is necessary for singing (Nottebohm et al., 1976)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nottebohm et al., 1976

claim: HVC exhibits neural activity precisely time-locked to song.
source: HVC, which is necessary for singing (Nottebohm et al., 1976), exhibits neural activity precisely time-locked to song (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Prather et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: HVC receives input from auditory regions that contain auditory feedback-sensitive neurons.
source: HVC, which is necessary for singing (Nottebohm et al., 1976), exhibits neural activity precisely time-locked to song (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Prather et al., 2008), and receives input from auditory regions that contain auditory feedback-sensitive neurons (Keller and Hahnloser, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Keller and Hahnloser, 2009

claim: HVCX neurons provide input to the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP).
source: Within HVC, a distinct type of projection neuron (HVCX) provides input to an anterior forebrain pathway (AFP)
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: The AFP is necessary for song learning.
source: Within HVC, a distinct type of projection neuron (HVCX) provides input to an anterior forebrain pathway (AFP) that is necessary for song learning
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: The AFP is anatomically similar to cortico-basal ganglia pathways in mammals.
source: an anterior forebrain pathway (AFP) that is necessary for song learning and that is anatomically similar to cortico-basal ganglia pathways in mammals (Farries and Perkel, 2002; Doupe et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farries and Perkel, 2002; Doupe et al., 2005

claim: LMAN is the source of behavioral variations that can adaptively bias song in response to feedback perturbations.
source: Various studies have shown that the output nucleus of the AFP (the lateral magnocellular nucleus of the anterior nidopallium, or LMAN) is the source of behavioral variations that can adaptively bias song in response to feedback perturbations (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Warren et al., 2011; Charlesworth et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: LMAN lesions prevent deafening-induced song degradation.
source: Specifically, LMAN lesions prevent deafening-induced song degradation (Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Warren et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Inactivating LMAN can reverse shifts in syllable pitch induced by distorted auditory feedback.
source: inactivating LMAN can reverse shifts in syllable pitch induced by distorted auditory feedback (DAF) (Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Warren et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Auditory responses detected in the AFP of anesthetized birds disappear when HVC is pharmacologically inactivated.
source: auditory responses that can be detected in the AFP of anesthetized birds disappear when HVC is pharmacologically inactivated (Roy and Mooney, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Roy and Mooney, 2009

claim: Individual HVCX cells can fire in remarkably similar patterns during singing and in response to song playback.
source: Moreover, individual HVCX cells can fire in remarkably similar patterns during singing and in response to song playback (Prather et al., 2008; Fujimoto et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Prather et al., 2008; Fujimoto et al., 2011

claim: The singing-related action potential activity of HVCX cells does not change when auditory feedback is masked by noise bursts.
source: However, the singing-related action potential activity of HVCX cells does not change when auditory feedback is masked by noise bursts (Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Prather et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Prather et al., 2008

claim: Deafening shrinks and destabilizes dendritic spines on HVCX neurons within approximately 12-48 hours.
source: a recent imaging study found that deafening shrinks and destabilizes dendritic spines on HVCX neurons within ∼12–48 hr, and these changes precede and predict the severity of song degradation (Tschida and Mooney, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tschida and Mooney, 2012

claim: Deafening-induced changes to HVCX dendritic spines precede and predict the severity of song degradation.
source: a recent imaging study found that deafening shrinks and destabilizes dendritic spines on HVCX neurons within ∼12–48 hr, and these changes precede and predict the severity of song degradation (Tschida and Mooney, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tschida and Mooney, 2012

claim: Distorted auditory feedback (DAF) failed to perturb singing-related synaptic activity of HVCX cells.
source: Using intracellular recordings in singing zebra finches, we found that DAF failed to perturb singing-related synaptic activity of HVCX cells
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Many HVCX cells responded to auditory stimuli in non-singing states.
source: Using intracellular recordings in singing zebra finches, we found that DAF failed to perturb singing-related synaptic activity of HVCX cells, although many of these cells responded to auditory stimuli in non-singing states
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Deafening-induced changes to HVCX synapses require intact AFP output.
source: Moreover, in vivo multiphoton imaging revealed that deafening-induced changes to HVCX synapses require intact AFP output
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: The AFP accesses feedback independent of HVC.
source: These findings support a model in which the AFP accesses feedback independent of HVC
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Songbirds use auditory feedback to learn and maintain their vocalizations.
source: Songbirds use auditory feedback to learn and maintain their vocalizations (Konishi, 1965; Price, 1979)
evidence: Supported by citations to Konishi, 1965; Price, 1979

claim: A total of 72 HVCX neurons were recorded from 11 birds.
source: We recorded from a total of 72 HVCX neurons in 11 birds as they engaged in spontaneous bouts of singing produced in social isolation (i.e., undirected song) and/or listened to playback of the bird's own song (BOS)
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail from the current study

claim: HVCX cells were identified by antidromic stimulation methods, DC current-evoked firing patterns, or characteristic singing-related hyperpolarization.
source: HVCX cells were identified either by antidromic stimulation methods (Figure 1A,B), DC current-evoked firing patterns (Mooney, 2000), or characteristic singing-related hyperpolarization (Long et al., 2010)
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail from the current study with citations

claim: All HVCX cells recorded showed spontaneous, regular action potential activity when the bird was not vocalizing at 8.2 ± 5.8 Hz.
source: As previously reported (Long et al., 2010), all HVCX cells we recorded without current injection showed spontaneous, regular action potential activity when the bird was not vocalizing (8.2 ± 5.8 Hz, mean ±SD)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with citation to prior work

claim: HVCX cells entered a hyperpolarized state within several hundred milliseconds before song onset.
source: all HVCX cells we recorded without current injection showed spontaneous, regular action potential activity when the bird was not vocalizing (8.2 ± 5.8 Hz, mean ±SD), entered a hyperpolarized state within several hundred milliseconds before song onset (baseline −58.5 ± 7.1 mV, during singing −62.3 ± 7.3 mV)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: All except two HVCX cells exhibited one or more action potential bursts during the utterance of the song motif.
source: all except two exhibited one or more action potential bursts during the utterance of the stereotyped sequence of syllables constituting the song motif (Figure 1D, Video 1)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure and video

claim: Each HVCX cell's pattern of subthreshold membrane potential activity and action potential bursts were highly stereotyped from one motif to the next and from bout to bout.
source: Each cell's pattern of subthreshold membrane potential activity (Vm) and action potential bursts were highly stereotyped from one motif to the next and from bout to bout (Figure 1D)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: As a population, HVCX cells exhibited no systematic changes in ΔVm or dPSP onset times in the presence of DAF.
source: As a population, HVCX cells exhibited no systematic changes in ΔVm or dPSP onset times in the presence of DAF (Figure 2B–D; n = 34 cells)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: None of the HVCX cells showed changes in dPSP onset times when treated on a cell-by-cell basis.
source: When treated on a cell-by-cell basis, none showed changes in dPSP onset times
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Only two HVCX cells showed slight (<1 mV) but significant changes in ΔVm.
source: only two cells showed slight (<1 mV) but significant changes in ΔVm (0.01 ≤ p<0.05; see Figure 2A, right, for one of these positive cases)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: Fast synaptic inputs onto HVCX neurons are insensitive to auditory feedback perturbation during singing.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that fast synaptic inputs onto HVCX neurons are insensitive to auditory feedback perturbation during singing
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: 7 out of 8 DAF-insensitive HVCX cells showed significant subthreshold responses to BOS playback during the day.
source: However, we found that DAF-insensitive HVCX cells could respond to auditory presentation of the bird's own song during periods when the bird was not singing, including during the daytime or minutes to hours into the night (Figure 3A–B; 7/8 DAF-insensitive cells showed significant subthreshold responses to BOS playback during the day
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: 4 out of 4 DAF-insensitive HVCX cells tracked across the day-night boundary showed significant sub- and suprathreshold responses during darkness.
source: 4/4 DAF-insensitive cells that we tracked across the day–night boundary showed significant sub- and suprathreshold responses during darkness)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: The majority of HVCX cells displayed BOS-evoked auditory activity during the day or night.
source: Moreover, the majority of HVCX cells we recorded from, including those in which we did not collect singing-related activity, displayed BOS-evoked auditory activity during the day or night (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, subthreshold responses: n = 15/27 cells in day; 10/11 cells in night; suprathreshold responses: 5/12 cells in day; 7/8 cells in night)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure supplement

claim: Auditory responses in the zebra finch HVC are strongly state-dependent.
source: Indeed, the increased proportion of auditory-responsive HVCX cells we detected during the night is consistent with prior extracellular studies that show auditory responses in the zebra finch HVC are strongly state-dependent (Cardin and Schmidt, 2003; Rauske et al., 2003; Nick and Konishi, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Longer intracellular recordings revealed clear evidence of auditory-vocal mirroring in two DAF-insensitive HVCX cells.
source: Although prior studies have not described auditory–vocal mirroring in HVC of zebra finches, longer intracellular recordings (>3 hr) that we made in two DAF-insensitive HVCX cells revealed clear evidence of auditory–vocal mirroring (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: BOS-evoked sub- and supra-threshold activity closely resembled the singing-related activity recorded earlier during the daytime in two HVCX cells.
source: Specifically, at later times during the night, we detected BOS-evoked sub- and supra-threshold activity that closely resembled the singing-related activity recorded earlier during the daytime
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: The correlation in membrane potential activity recorded during singing and in response to BOS playback increased at later times in the night.
source: Moreover, in a larger subset of HVCX cells in which we recorded singing-related activity with or without DAF during the day and tracked across the day–night boundary, we found that the correlation in membrane potential activity recorded during singing and in response to BOS playback increased at later times in the night (Figure 4C)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: Auditory-vocal mirror neurons in the zebra finch HVC are insensitive to auditory feedback perturbation during singing.
source: These findings show that auditory–vocal mirror neurons in the zebra finch HVC are insensitive to auditory feedback perturbation during singing
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Sensorimotor mirroring may be a latent feature of a large cohort of HVCX cells in zebra finches.
source: These findings show that auditory–vocal mirror neurons in the zebra finch HVC are insensitive to auditory feedback perturbation during singing and also suggest that sensorimotor mirroring may be a latent feature of a large cohort of HVCX cells in this species
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Most (5/9) HVC shelf cells showed significantly greater subthreshold depolarizing responses in the presence of DAF.
source: During singing, we found that most (5/9) HVC shelf cells showed significantly greater subthreshold depolarizing responses in the presence of DAF, consistent with the notion that they receive synaptic input from neurons that exhibit DAF-sensitive action potential output (Figure 5A,C, D
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: One HVC shelf cell showed a significant suprathreshold response to DAF.
source: one of these cells also showed a significant suprathreshold response to DAF, Figure 5B)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: Synaptic activity in HVC shelf cells can be modulated during singing.
source: These recordings also revealed that synaptic activity in HVC shelf cells can be modulated during singing
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: The pattern of synaptic activity in HVC shelf cells was less stereotyped from one motif to the next than observed in HVCX cells.
source: although the pattern of this activity was less stereotyped from one motif to the next than observed in HVCX cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B. HVC shelf: n = 14 cells, C.C. = 0.12 ± 0.03 (SEM). HVCX cells: n = 53 cells, C.C. = 0.70 ± 0.02, without time warping)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure supplement

claim: The intracellular recording technique can detect subthreshold membrane potential responses to DAF in the singing zebra finch.
source: These data confirm that the intracellular recording technique used here can detect subthreshold membrane potential responses to DAF in the singing zebra finch
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Auditory-related synaptic inputs to HVCX cells are gated in an 'off' position during singing.
source: These data confirm that the intracellular recording technique used here can detect subthreshold membrane potential responses to DAF in the singing zebra finch, further strengthening the idea that auditory-related synaptic inputs to HVCX cells are gated in an 'off' position during singing
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: dPSP onsets in HVCX cells occur on average approximately 25 ms before syllable onsets.
source: Population-averaged cross-correlation analysis revealed that dPSP onsets in HVCX cells occur on average ∼25 ms before syllable onsets (n = 53 cells, Figure 6D)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: dPSP onsets were not correlated with syllable offsets.
source: In contrast, dPSP onsets were not correlated with syllable offsets (Figure 6D)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: Singing-related synaptic inputs to HVCX cells are correlated to future, rather than ongoing or past, vocal output.
source: In contrast, dPSP onsets were not correlated with syllable offsets (Figure 6D), indicating that singing-related synaptic inputs to HVCX cells are correlated to future, rather than ongoing or past, vocal output
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings with reference to figure

claim: Significant changes in membrane potential fluctuations of HVCX cells were observed when DAF triggered song truncation or delays in syllable onsets.
source: In fact, we observed significant changes in membrane potential fluctuations of HVCX cells when DAF-triggered song truncation or delays in syllable onsets (Figure 6F,H)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure

claim: The intracellular method is capable of detecting DAF-related changes in the subthreshold activity of HVCX cells, but only when DAF triggers acute vocal motor effects.
source: Therefore, the intracellular method we used is capable of detecting DAF-related changes in the subthreshold activity of HVCX cells, but only when DAF triggers acute vocal motor effects
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Synaptic inputs to HVCX cells do not convey auditory feedback signals during singing and instead encode information about future vocal output, consistent with a motor-related signal.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that synaptic inputs to HVCX cells do not convey auditory feedback signals during singing and instead encode information about future vocal output, consistent with a motor-related signal
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: LMAN lesions prevent the decrease in HVCX cell spine size index that normally follows deafening.
source: Surprisingly, in addition to greatly reducing song degradation, LMAN lesions completely prevented the decrease in HVCX cell spine size index that normally follows deafening (Figure 8B–C; 471 spines from 7 HVCX neurons in 3 LMAN lesion-deafened birds; 495 spines from 7 HVCX cells in 6 LMAN-intact deafened birds; spine data from LMAN intact-deafened birds were previously reported in Tschida and Mooney, 2012; p=0.001 for difference between groups across all time bins)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure and statistical analysis

claim: Post-deafening spine size index values from HVCX cells in deafened birds with LMAN lesions did not differ from values measured from longitudinally imaged birds with normal hearing.
source: In fact, the post-deafening spine size index values from HVCX cells in deafened birds with LMAN lesions measured here did not differ from values measured from longitudinally imaged birds with normal hearing (data not shown; spine data from birds with normal hearing were previously reported in Tschida and Mooney, 2012)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with citation

claim: Lesions to LMAN prevented deafening-induced decreases in HVCX cell spine stability.
source: Lesions to LMAN also prevented deafening-induced decreases in HVCX cell spine stability, and spine stability measurements from HVCX cells in LMAN lesion-deafened birds were significantly higher than those from LMAN intact-deafened HVCX cells in all post-song degradation time bins (Figure 8C; 2401 spines from 7 HVCX cells in 3 LMAN lesion-deafened birds; 3562 spines from 14 HVCX cells in 9 LMAN intact-deafened birds; spine data from LMAN intact-deafened birds were previously reported in Tschida and Mooney, 2012; p≤0.02 for difference between groups in last 3 time bins)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure and statistical analysis

claim: Deafening-induced changes to dendritic spines on HVCX cells depend on an intact LMAN.
source: Therefore, in contrast to a feedforward model of auditory feedback processing by HVC, deafening-induced changes to dendritic spines on HVCX cells depend on an intact LMAN
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Spine dynamics in HVCX cells following LMAN lesions but prior to deafening did not differ from values obtained from similarly aged birds with normal hearing and an intact LMAN.
source: First, spine dynamics in HVCX cells following LMAN lesions but prior to deafening did not differ from values obtained from similarly aged birds with normal hearing and an intact LMAN (Figure 9A; HVCX cell spine size index: 1.10 ± 0.06 in LMAN lesion group; 1.07 ± 0.03 in LMAN intact group, mean ±SEM, p=0.62; HVCX cell spine stability: 94.0 ± 1.1% in LMAN lesion group, 92.0 ± 1.6% in LMAN intact group, p=0.61; LMAN intact data previously reported in Tschida and Mooney, 2012)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure and statistical analysis

claim: Prior to deafening, LMAN lesions did not affect the mean or variability of syllable entropy or entropy variance (EV).
source: Second, prior to deafening, LMAN lesions did not affect the mean or variability of syllable entropy or entropy variance (EV), two features that are sensitive to small changes in song's acoustic structure (Figure 9B; Wilcoxon signed-ranks test used to compare pre-lesion to post-lesion values for 25 syllables from 6 birds [includes 3 birds used for imaging]; data shown only for mean entropy and EV; p=0.09 for mean entropy, p=0.92 for coefficient of variation [CV] of entropy, p=0.25 for mean EV, p=0.31 for CV of EV)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure and statistical analysis

claim: The lesions made in LMAN were comparable in volume to those reported in previous studies that have established LMAN's role in preventing deafening-induced song degradation.
source: Third, a post mortem analysis of brain tissue indicated that the lesions we made in LMAN were comparable in volume to those reported in previous studies that have established LMAN's role in preventing deafening-induced song degradation (40–100% lesion extent, Brainard and Doupe, 2000)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with citation

claim: Birds that received LMAN lesions still showed extremely subtle but significant song degradation following deafening.
source: Finally, although the LMAN lesions we made largely prevented deafening-induced song degradation, birds that received LMAN lesions still showed extremely subtle but significant song degradation following deafening, as previously reported (Figure 8A) (Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Horita et al., 2008)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure and citations

claim: Neither the complete abolition of auditory feedback by deafening nor the expression of small amounts of deafening-induced vocal plasticity in LMAN-lesioned birds are sufficient to drive structural changes to HVC dendritic spines.
source: Therefore, neither the complete abolition of auditory feedback by deafening nor the expression of small amounts of deafening-induced vocal plasticity in LMAN-lesioned birds are sufficient to drive structural changes to HVC dendritic spines
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Singing-related synaptic activity in HVCX neurons lacks real-time sensitivity to feedback perturbation.
source: By directly measuring synaptic activity in singing birds, we found that singing-related synaptic activity in HVCX neurons lacks real-time sensitivity to feedback perturbation
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Many HVCX cells displayed auditory responses in non-singing states, including a subset of cells that exhibited auditory-motor mirroring.
source: Moreover, many HVCX cells that we recorded displayed auditory responses in non-singing states, including a subset of cells that exhibited auditory-motor mirroring
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Although HVCX cells receive fast synaptic inputs from several sources that may have the potential to convey auditory feedback during singing, these inputs appear to be gated to an 'off' position during vocalization in zebra finches.
source: Therefore, although HVCX cells receive fast synaptic inputs from several sources that may have the potential to convey auditory feedback during singing, these inputs appear to be gated to an 'off' position during vocalization in zebra finches (Shea and Margoliash, 2003; Cardin and Schmidt, 2004; Coleman et al., 2007)
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings with citations

claim: The hit rate for applying DAF used during intracellular recordings (approximately 50%) has been shown to be sufficiently frequent to drive adaptive changes in pitch.
source: First, the hit rate for applying DAF we used during intracellular recordings (i.e., ∼50%) has been shown here (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and by others to be sufficiently frequent to drive adaptive changes in pitch (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Charlesworth et al., 2012; Ali et al., 2013)
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study with reference to figure supplement and citations

claim: All of the analyses of subthreshold DAF sensitivity were conducted after the bird had been exposed to DAF for at least an entire preceding day.
source: Second, all of the analyses of subthreshold DAF sensitivity we performed were conducted after the bird had been exposed to DAF for at least an entire preceding day, the time required for the bird to habituate to the exposure, as determined by the decreased frequency of song truncations we observed in response to DAF
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail from the current study

claim: Singing-related HVC multiunit activity remains unchanged even after contingent DAF is used to drive changes in song pitch.
source: And although we did not track any single cell's activity while DAF exposure induced song plasticity, a recent study by Ali et al. (2013) has shown that singing-related HVC multiunit activity remains unchanged even after contingent DAF is used to drive changes in song pitch
evidence: Supported by citation to Ali et al., 2013

claim: Auditory synapses onto HVCX cells are always gated off when the bird is singing.
source: Therefore, we support a model in which auditory synapses onto HVCX cells are always gated off when the bird is singing
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Deafening-induced changes to HVCX spines depend on an intact AFP, rather than resulting simply from the removal of auditory drive to HVC.
source: In contrast, we found that LMAN lesions prevent the shrinkage and destabilization of HVCX dendritic spines that normally follow deafening. Therefore, deafening-induced changes to HVCX spines depend on an intact AFP, rather than resulting simply from the removal of auditory drive to HVC
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Deafening-induced synaptic changes in HVCX cells are a consequence rather than a cause of error correction processes mediated by the AFP.
source: Although the current experiments cannot resolve whether deafening-induced changes in HVC are driven solely by changes in LMAN activity or instead by LMAN acting in concert with the removal of auditory inputs to HVCX cells, the total insensitivity of HVCX cells to acute feedback perturbations suggests to us that deafening-induced synaptic changes in HVCX cells are a consequence rather than a cause of error correction processes mediated by the AFP
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: The indirect, recurrent pathways that can convey activity from LMAN to HVC provide a substrate over which the consequences of error correction processes in the AFP could be transmitted back to the early stages of the vocal motor hierarchy.
source: The indirect, recurrent pathways that can convey activity from LMAN to HVC (Hamaguchi and Mooney, 2012) provide a substrate over which the consequences of error correction processes in the AFP could be transmitted back to the early stages of the vocal motor hierarchy
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings with citation

claim: LMAN can access multiple stages of the motor hierarchy in tens of milliseconds.
source: Furthermore, because LMAN can access multiple stages of the motor hierarchy in tens of milliseconds (Hamaguchi and Mooney, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamaguchi and Mooney, 2012

claim: The consequences of performance evaluation may be widely distributed in the song motor network even before behavioral changes are first evident.
source: Furthermore, because LMAN can access multiple stages of the motor hierarchy in tens of milliseconds (Hamaguchi and Mooney, 2012) and song may only change in response to altered feedback over hours or days, the consequences of performance evaluation may be widely distributed in the song motor network even before behavioral changes are first evident
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings with citation

claim: Input and output cells of the AFP (HVCX and LMAN neurons) are not real-time sensors of auditory feedback.
source: Previous studies have shown that input and output cells of the AFP (HVCX and LMAN neurons) are not real-time sensors of auditory feedback (Leonardo, 2004; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Prather et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Feedback-dependent changes that can be detected in HVC depend on the AFP rather than fast synaptic signaling onto HVCX cells from feedback-sensing auditory neurons.
source: the current study shows that even those feedback-dependent changes that can be detected in HVC depend on the AFP rather than fast synaptic signaling onto HVCX cells from feedback-sensing auditory neurons
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: HVC is downstream of the performance evaluation provided by real-time feedback sensors.
source: These findings suggest that HVC is downstream of the performance evaluation provided by real-time feedback sensors
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: Real-time feedback sensors may communicate error-related information to the AFP independent of HVC.
source: These findings suggest that HVC is downstream of the performance evaluation provided by real-time feedback sensors, and also raises the possibility that these sensors communicate error-related information to the AFP independent of HVC
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the current study's findings

claim: The ventral tegmental area provides input to Area X.
source: Notably, the ventral tegmental area provides input to Area X (Lewis et al., 1981)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lewis et al., 1981

claim: The ventral tegmental area receives indirect input from several auditory regions, including the HVC shelf, that contain DAF-sensitive cells.
source: Notably, the ventral tegmental area provides input to Area X (Lewis et al., 1981) and receives indirect input from several auditory regions, including the HVC shelf, that contain DAF-sensitive cells (Wild et al., 1993; Fortune and Margoliash, 1995; Vates et al., 1996; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The consequences of error detection may reach the AFP in the form of neuromodulatory signals from the VTA.
source: In this scenario, the consequences of error detection would reach the AFP in the form of neuromodulatory signals from the VTA
evidence: Stated as a speculative scenario

claim: A buffered feedback architecture, along with the gating of auditory inputs to HVC, may be necessary when the frequency of motor control is so fast that a relatively slow feedback signal becomes uninformative for the ongoing motor command.
source: In fact, this buffered feedback architecture, along with the gating of auditory inputs to HVC, may be necessary when the frequency of motor control is so fast that a relatively slow feedback signal becomes uninformative for the ongoing motor command
evidence: Stated as a speculative conclusion
